section_title: A Daughter Restored and a Woman Made Well

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 21 When Jesus had again crossed by boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around Him beside the sea. 22 A synagogue leader named Jairus arrived, and seeing Jesus, he fell at His feet 23 and pleaded with Him urgently, “My little daughter is near death. Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” 24 So Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around Him.

25 And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. 26 She had borne much agony under the care of many physicians and had spent all she had, but to no avail. Instead, her condition had only grown worse. 27 When the woman heard about Jesus, she came up through the crowd behind Him and touched His cloak. 28 For she kept saying, “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” 29 Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she sensed in her body that she was healed of her affliction.

30 At once Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him. Turning to the crowd, He asked, “Who touched My garments?” 31 His disciples answered, “You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’ ” 32 But He kept looking around to see who had done this. 33 Then the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before Him trembling in fear, and she told Him the whole truth. 34 “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.”

35 While He was still speaking, messengers from the house of Jairus arrived and said, “Your daughter is dead; why bother the Teacher anymore?” 36 But Jesus overheard their conversation and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” 37 And He did not allow anyone to accompany Him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. 38 When they arrived at the house of the synagogue leader, Jesus saw the commotion and the people weeping and wailing loudly. 39 He went inside and asked, “Why all this commotion and weeping? The child is not dead, but asleep.” 40 And they laughed at Him. After He had put them all outside, He took the child’s father and mother and His own companions, and went in to see the child.

41 Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” 42 Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around (she was twelve years old). And at once they were utterly astounded. 43 Then Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about this, and He told them to give her something to eat.

context_lines: Back across the sea, Jairus, a synagogue leader, asks Jesus to save his dying daughter. Jesus goes with him, but another person's need interrupts the journey. Mark places the woman's healing inside the daughter's story, letting us follow Jairus through a delay before the outcome at his home.

The woman has bled for twelve years, spent everything seeking treatment, and grown worse. After hearing about Jesus, she comes through the crowd and touches His cloak. [Leviticus 15:19,25–30](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/15.htm) describes the ritual uncleanness connected with ongoing bleeding, which helps explain the wider burden of her condition. That law does not tell us she caused her illness through a particular personal sin.

Her bleeding stops. Jesus knows power has gone out from Him and asks who touched His garments. The woman comes forward in fear and tells Him the truth; He addresses her as daughter, credits her faith, and sends her in peace. The verb σῴζω, *sōzō* (SOH-zoh), can mean to save or rescue, and here to heal. [Thayer's lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/4982.htm) specifically includes her healing and Jairus's request. The word's wider range does not make the bodily cure less real.

While Jesus speaks, messengers announce the girl's death. Jesus tells Jairus not to fear but to believe. At the house He admits the parents and Peter, James, and John, takes the child by the hand, and tells her to rise. Mark preserves His words, Talitha koum, and immediately supplies their meaning. The girl gets up and walks, and Jesus asks that she be given food.

Calling her asleep is not the narrator denying the reported death. [Luke 8:49–55](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/8.htm) says the people know she is dead and describes her spirit returning. Jesus treats as temporary a condition the messengers regard as the end of hope. The girl is twelve, matching the length of the woman's suffering; Mark draws the stories together without explaining the number as a hidden code.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly see the two stories as calls to trust Jesus and as displays of His authority to heal and restore life. [Calvin on Matthew 9:20–22 and Mark 5:39–41](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/5.htm) and the [US Catholic bishops' notes on Mark 5:28,35,39](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/5) connect the healings with faith and understand the girl's sleep language in relation to death from which Jesus raises her, rather than an ordinary nap.
god_plan_lines: Both stories bring Jesus close to conditions Israel's law associates with uncleanness: ongoing bleeding in Leviticus 15 and contact with the dead in [Numbers 19:11–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/19.htm). The focus of the encounter is restoration. The woman is healed, and the child is alive and eating.

The New Testament carries cleansing into a deeper saving purpose. [Hebrews 9:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/9.htm) compares the earlier cleansing rites with Christ's own offering, which purifies the conscience for serving God. [Romans 5:6–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/5.htm) describes His death and life bringing reconciliation when people were powerless and estranged. These are wider scriptural connections, not claims that every detail of the two miracles predicts a separate event.

The girl's restoration also points us toward the larger hope beyond death. [1 Corinthians 15:20–23,50–57](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm) grounds that hope in Christ's resurrection and promises an imperishable life to those who belong to Him. Jairus's daughter returns to ordinary life here; the final victory over death reaches beyond this one rescue.
current_position_lines: For the woman's healing, we draw from Prayer and Faith, which uses the parallel Matthew 9:20–22 to emphasize faith in Jesus over the wording of a request. She reaches out to Him before making a spoken request for healing. Mark also records her later conversation with Him, so this does not mean she remains silent throughout the encounter. Our point here is the trust Jesus credits, not a formula for producing a miracle. We have not developed a separate position on Jairus's part of the passage.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Section 5, Faith, Not Petition, Is What Scripture Emphasizes; narrowly the woman’s faith preceding a spoken healing request in the parallel Matthew9:20–22. Does not extend its silence claim beyond the healing or originate a Jairus position.
